subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: I'm Vishal, Rajni's neighbour on the third floor. Her son Bittu is four. Whenever anyone speaks to him in the lift, Rajni answers first: "He's the shy one, he won't talk." Yesterday the watchman asked Bittu his name. Bittu opened his mouth, and Rajni said, "Bittu. Sorry, he's very shy." Bittu closed his mouth and hid behind her dupatta. At the building's Holi party, she kept him on her lap instead of letting him join the water-balloon game, saying he'd hate it. Yet I've seen Bittu chatter to my dog through the balcony railing for ten minutes straight. I don't know what goes on in either of their heads. But I wonder if he's learning that his voice isn't needed.

qa.q: What did Bittu chatter to through the balcony railing?
qa.a: Vishal's dog.

qa.q: What does Rajni answering for Bittu suggest about how she sees him?
qa.a: She seems sure he's "the shy one" who won't talk, so she steps in before he gets a chance, perhaps to protect him.

qa.q: What could Rajni try the next time someone speaks to Bittu in the lift?
qa.a: She could wait quietly and give him time to answer himself, even slowly, showing she expects he can.

qa.q: How might being called "the shy one" feel to Bittu over time?
qa.a: He might start to believe his voice isn't needed and hide more, even though he clearly chatters away when nobody is labelling him.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young mother convinced her son is the shy one answer for him and keep him from chances, so he plays the role.

passage:
Monday: At the school gate, Kiran's teacher asked her about the weekend. Baljeet answered for her, as always. "She's the shy one, ma'am." Kiran, five, stared at her shoes.
Thursday: At her cousin's birthday party, the magician asked for a helper. Kiran's hand twitched upward. Baljeet caught it gently. "You won't like it, beta." She sat back and watched the other children laugh on stage.
Next Monday: Baljeet had spent the weekend thinking about that twitching hand. At the gate, when the teacher asked about the weekend, he said nothing. The silence felt long. Then Kiran whispered, "We went to the lake." Then, louder, "There was a duck with no tail!"

qa.q: What did Kiran say about the duck?
qa.a: There was a duck with no tail.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet keep thinking about Kiran's twitching hand over the weekend?
qa.a: He seemed to realise she had wanted to volunteer, and that his certainty that she was "the shy one" had held her back.

qa.q: What choice did Baljeet make the next Monday, and what did it show?
qa.a: He stayed silent and let Kiran answer herself; given room and time, she spoke, first in a whisper and then louder. 😊

qa.q: What might Thursday's party have felt like for Kiran?
qa.a: Her hand showed she wanted to go up, so being held back while other children laughed on stage may have felt disappointing and taught her again that she is the one who watches.

grounding: A young father sure his daughter is the shy one answers for her and holds her back, until he gives her room and she begins to speak.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: Anand, you keep telling people little Meenu is "the shy one." Your old father Tarun has made that mistake before, so listen. When I was twenty-five and your sister Sunita was three, I decided the same about her. At every wedding I answered for her: "Sunita doesn't dance, she's shy." When the school wanted her in the annual-day play, I said no before she could speak. And she became exactly what I said: quiet, always behind a pillar. Then your mother went to her village for a month, and I was alone with Sunita. With nobody speaking for her, she ordered at the sweet shop, argued with the milkman, sang in the bath. I had been building her a small room and calling it her nature. Today Sunita teaches a class of forty. Give Meenu some room.

qa.q: What did young Tarun say at weddings about Sunita?
qa.a: "Sunita doesn't dance, she's shy."

qa.q: What did Tarun realise during the month alone with Sunita?
qa.a: He realised that by answering for her he had been "building her a small room" and calling it her nature, since without him speaking for her she ordered, argued and sang.

qa.q: What choice is Tarun asking Anand to make now?
qa.a: To stop calling Meenu "the shy one" and give her room to speak and try things herself, instead of answering for her.

qa.q: How might Sunita have experienced being "the shy one" as a child?
qa.a: Her father kept speaking and refusing for her, so she may have felt there was no space to try, and quietly became the girl behind the pillar.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a young father sure his daughter was shy, he answered for her and she adopted the role until she was given room.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: The overnight train to Kochi was packed and noisy, and Thomas, twenty-six, had his five-year-old son Chinmay tucked beside him on the lower berth. When the ticket checker smiled and asked, 'What's your name, little one?' Thomas answered, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.' Chinmay pressed into his father's side. Across the aisle, three children were playing snap. 'Want to play?' a girl called. 'He doesn't like joining in,' Thomas said. Then his office phone rang, and it was his boss, and the connection kept dropping. He went to the door end of the coach to hear. It took twenty minutes. When he came back, Chinmay was sitting cross-legged in the middle of the other berth, slapping cards down. 'I'm Chinmay! I won two!' Thomas stood in the aisle holding his phone, suddenly unsure which of them had been shy.

qa.q: What did Thomas tell the ticket checker?
qa.a: Thomas said, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.'

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he came back and saw Chinmay playing?
qa.a: He felt surprised and unsure, starting to wonder whether the 'shy one' label was really about Chinmay or about his own belief.

qa.q: What could Thomas try the next time someone asks Chinmay a question?
qa.a: He could wait and let Chinmay answer for himself, and let him decide whether to join games, instead of saying no for him.

qa.q: How might the girl who invited Chinmay see him now?
qa.a: She probably sees him as a fun, chatty player who likes winning at snap, not a shy child at all.

grounding: A young father sure his son is shy answers for him and turns down invitations, until a work call leaves the boy alone and he joins in by himself.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: At the Diwali rangoli contest in their Gurugram apartment society, Sunaina held six-year-old Vikas's hand tightly. 'He's my shy one,' she told the organiser. 'He'll just watch.' The organiser offered Vikas a bowl of orange powder. Vikas looked at it for a long time. 'He doesn't like crowds,' Sunaina said, and gently moved the bowl away. At the snack table, when an aunty asked Vikas what class he was in, Sunaina said, 'First standard. He's quiet.' Vikas nodded. Later, his grandfather found him staring at the other children's patterns. 'Want to try, beta?' Vikas shook his head. 'I'm shy,' he said, very seriously. 'Mumma says.' Sunaina laughed and ruffled his hair. But that night, clearing up, she found a small orange handprint on the corner of the contest sheet, and nobody else's hand was that size.

qa.q: What did the organiser offer Vikas?
qa.a: The organiser offered Vikas a bowl of orange powder.

qa.q: What does the small orange handprint suggest about Vikas?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to join in more than he showed, and that the 'shy' label may be holding him back rather than describing him.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do differently at the next event?
qa.a: She could let Vikas answer questions himself and let him take the bowl of powder if he wants, giving him room to try.

qa.q: How might Vikas's grandfather see what is happening?
qa.a: His grandfather may notice that Vikas repeats 'Mumma says' and worry that the boy is learning to be shy from what he hears.

grounding: A young mother sure her son is the shy one answers for him and keeps him from joining, and he starts repeating the label, though a small handprint hints he wanted to take part.
